chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Musa ibn Sa'dan, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Umar ibn Yazeed, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'By Allah, I do not know whether my father performed the Aqeeqa for me or not.' He said, 'So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) ordered me, and I performed the Aqeeqa for myself, and I am an old man.'
And Umar said, 'I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: Every person is pledged with his Aqeeqa, and the Aqeeqa is more obligatory than the Udhiyah (sacrifice).'

key_terms.الْأُضْحِيَّةِ: Udhiyah, the sacrificial animal offered during Eid al-Adha
key_terms.عَقِيقَتِهِ: Aqeeqa, the ritual sacrifice made for a newborn child
key_terms.مُرْتَهَنٌ: Pledged / held in pledge (referring to the soul being held until Aqeeqa is performed)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Aqeeqa if one is unsure if their father performed it, and how does it compare to Udhiyah?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the legal principle of 'al-mar'u murtaqan bi-aqeeqatihi' (every person is pledged by their Aqeeqa), establishing that the obligation remains on the individual until fulfilled. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) specifies that if the father's performance is uncertain, the adult must perform it for themselves, highlighting its status as a more binding obligation than the Eid Udhiyah. This underscores the Aqeeqa's role in spiritual purification and gratitude, linking the newborn's entry into the community with a tangible act of worship.
